title: I asked 100 companies for my data. Some deleted it instead.
gist: A reporter's experiment filing over 100 CCPA data-access requests found that companies like Crunchbase and BeenVerified repeatedly misclassified access requests as deletion requests despite explicit instructions otherwise, and Cash App's phone support couldn't process a request its own privacy policy said the channel supports, illustrating widespread, likely under-resourced compliance failures under California's privacy law.

themes.theme: CCPA access requests fail in practice

insights.claim: Under the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), which took effect in 2020, California residents have the right to request access to, deletion of, and opt-out of the sale of their personal data, and companies generally have up to 45 days to fulfill an access request.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Establishes the legal baseline against which the article's compliance failures are measured, relevant to any company operating in California's consumer data market.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The CCPA went into effect in 2020'

insights.claim: A CCPA access request to McDonald's returned a 515-page report detailing the requester's app interactions in granular detail, including a prediction that they would never stop eating there.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Illustrates how deep behavioral profiling and predictive modeling on consumer app usage has become even at a fast-food chain, a data point on the scale of first-party data collection outside traditional tech companies.

insights.claim: Ben Winters, director of AI and privacy at the Consumer Federation of America, says companies mishandling access requests as deletions is not an acceptable status quo and reflects the core weakness of privacy policy frameworks that rely on companies acting responsibly and in good faith.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Frames the compliance failures as a structural flaw in self-regulatory privacy law design, not isolated vendor mistakes, which is the argument for stronger enforcement or a different regulatory model.
insights.quote: That's crazy. That's not an acceptable status quo.

insights.claim: After the reporter emailed Crunchbase an access request that explicitly said 'do not treat this as a deletion request,' a support representative permanently deleted the reporter's Crunchbase account within two days, which the company later blamed on a 'processing error' by a human customer success team member, not an AI tool.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Shows a well-known B2B data company failing basic CCPA request handling even with an explicit written instruction not to delete, a reputational and legal-exposure data point for Crunchbase.
insights.quote: Thanks so much for your patience. Your account has been permanently deleted from Crunchbase. Please let me know if you need anything else!

insights.claim: BeenVerified repeatedly misclassified the reporter's access request as an opt-out/deletion request across multiple email exchanges, at one point denying it could verify the reporter's identity despite having already surfaced some of their personal details in the same thread.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A data broker whose core business is aggregating public records repeatedly failed to correctly process the one type of request (access, not deletion) it was explicitly asked to fulfill, suggesting systemic process gaps at a firm whose entire product is personal data handling.
insights.quote: Please be assured that we're able to process your opt-out request and have removed your information from our website.

insights.claim: BeenVerified's parent company said via its senior counsel that the support agent involved had received annual CCPA privacy training but was mistaken and misunderstood the request type, and the company now plans refresher training and an audit of recent work.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The company's own admission that formal training didn't prevent repeated misclassification points to a process or incentive failure rather than a knowledge gap, useful context for assessing compliance-remediation claims from data brokers generally.

insights.claim: Cash App's (Block's) privacy policy states California residents can file access requests via its website or a listed toll-free phone number, but calling that number produced agents unfamiliar with CCPA access requests, repeated holds, and instructions to call back later so the support team could review its own resources.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A discrepancy between a fintech's written privacy policy and what its phone support channel can actually execute is a compliance and consumer-trust risk specific to Cash App/Block.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'My attempts to place an access request with Cash App'

insights.claim: A Cash App spokesperson responded that customers can access or delete personal information directly through the app, which lets the company verify identity faster before releasing financial data, but did not address why the phone number is explicitly listed in its privacy policy as an access-request channel.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The company's response effectively concedes its printed privacy policy channel doesn't match operational reality, without correcting the policy or explaining the gap.
insights.quote: Customers can access or delete their personal information directly through Cash App, which allows us to more quickly verify identity before providing access to financial account information or deleting an account.

insights.claim: Elina van Kempen, a UC Irvine PhD student who co-authored a study of CCPA compliance across more than 500 data brokers, says she encountered the same pattern of automated responses treating access requests as opt-out or deletion requests, with mixed follow-through on corrections.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Independent academic research corroborates the reporter's anecdotal findings at much larger scale (500+ data brokers), indicating request misclassification is an industry-wide pattern, not isolated incidents.
insights.quote: Sometimes I would make an access request, and the automatic answer was 'We will opt you out' or 'We will delete your data.'

insights.claim: Mayu Tobin-Miyaji of the Electronic Privacy Information Center says the pattern of mishandled access requests shows how little resourcing companies devote to ensuring people can actually access their data.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Attributes the compliance failures to under-investment rather than technical difficulty, implying the fix is a resourcing or enforcement problem, not a hard engineering one.
insights.quote: It shows how potentially little resources the companies are putting toward compliance and making sure that people can have access to their data.

insights.claim: Both Ben Winters and Mayu Tobin-Miyaji point to 'data minimization' -- limiting what companies can collect in the first place to only what's needed for standard business operations -- as a more holistic fix than relying on consumers to file and chase access requests.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Data minimization is the policy alternative investors and compliance teams should watch for in future privacy legislation, since it shifts enforcement burden from reactive consumer requests to upfront collection limits.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Both Winters and Tobin-Miyaji mentioned'
